extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers; journalists and editors interested in international press freedom and wire-service reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of Associated Press international dispatches covering geopolitics, press censorship, humanitarian and technical topics; useful for editors compiling a news homepage or reporters summarizing global press conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding of news at the source
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts may be deliberately suppressed or announced only in part to fit propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs chiefly in dictatorships but can happen in democracies; sometimes done for 'military security' reasons. The survey notes this as a primary form of censorship — officials may deliberately omit unfavorable facts or release partial information to shape public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outgoing-dispatch censorship and correspondent restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: All dispatches for cabling abroad may be submitted through official clerks; foreign correspondents' shipments (film, photos) and movements can be curtailed and copy returned or delayed by censors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Soviet practice of requiring submission of outgoing copy through counter clerks, censorship rooms where copy is penciled out or held for hours/days, restrictions on flights/shipments of photos/film. Visa denial, forced departures, and spot checks/delays on outgoing copy are cited as common mechanisms affecting foreign news flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic press control via party/state mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic newspapers, radio and TV outlets are tightly controlled by government or party representatives acting as editors; publication of unauthorized information can be criminalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Eastern European communist states where party representatives serve as editors, jailing of journalists, suppression of theaters/restaurants/events, and use of special tribunals. Source censorship affects local reporters as well as foreign correspondents; publication of 'unsatisfactory' news can result in imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication (prior) censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories and pictures are subject to censorship before publication or broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted in Spain and Portugal historically; in some countries radio/TV scripts or outgoing network copy must be cleared first. In practice this means government review and deletion of material seen as unfavorable before it reaches the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization and legal penalties for press content
rubrics_metrics.description: Press laws impose penalties (fines, imprisonment, suspension of publication) for offenses such as belittling officials, publishing false news, or damaging public order or national financial standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Turkey's press laws (penalties up to 3 years' prison and a fine of 10,000 Turkish pounds for specified offenses). Other jurisdictions use fines, jail sentences, suppression orders, or suspension/closure of publications as enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional indicators for assessing press freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Press freedom assessments use a cluster of indicators — degree of source censorship, visa/access for correspondents, domestic control mechanisms, prepublication checks, and legal penalties — which vary by region and country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article summarizes regional patterns: Western Europe generally free (exceptions: Spain, Portugal); Eastern Europe under stringent controls and visa restrictions; Middle East and many Asian/African countries vary from tight control to relative freedom; Latin America shows mixed trends tied to political conditions. Use these indicators together to evaluate a country's press freedom status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics for public nutrition/dietary promotion campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques to stimulate interest and change dietary behavior: puppet shows, food-themed competitions, cooking demonstrations in marketplaces, choral/folk songs, mobile food wagons, school committees, curriculum integration, and local route/logistics planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples drawn from FAO campaigns: puppet shows and fish-painting competitions in Mexico; mobile fried-fish wagons in Brazil and Chile; forming town fish committees and school work units in Yugoslavia to establish supply routes and integrate subject matter into biology and home-economics classes. These practical, participatory methods are recommended to change tastes and increase acceptance of new foods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of closed/cleared briefings for classified subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings covering secret or sensitive information should be closed sessions and limited to cleared participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a five-day high-level symposium on medical problems connected with nuclear weapons: session closed due to secret information, all invited military and civilian medical experts cleared for secret material, and attendance limited to vetted personnel. Such procedural safeguards are noted as necessary when presentations involve classified military or national-security material.
